title: Mark and Toys
directAnswer: Maximise the COUNT of toys, not the money spent. Sort prices ascending, then walk left to right buying each toy while the running total stays within budget — the moment a toy would overshoot, stop. Sorting dominates at O(n log n); the buying scan is O(n).

remember.formula:
sort(prices)
total = 0; count = 0
for p in prices:
    if total + p > budget: break
    total += p; count += 1
return count
rules: You're maximising **how many** toys, not the total value — so spend on the cheapest items first.
Sort **ascending**, then take a prefix. The answer is always a prefix of the sorted array.
Use `break`, not `continue`, the first time a toy overshoots — every later toy is at least as expensive, so none can fit. (True only because the array is sorted.)
Add the price **before** incrementing the count, and check `total + p > budget` so you never count a toy you can't afford.
`total` can exceed `int` range if prices and n are large — use `long` in Java to be safe.
whenToUse: Maximise the number of items chosen under a single capacity/budget constraint
Each item has a cost but identical 'value' (you only care about the count)
No dependency between items — picking one doesn't change another's cost
The objective is a count, and items can be freely reordered
antiSignals: Items have different values, not just costs → that's 0/1 Knapsack (DP), not greedy
You must hit an exact budget, not stay under it → subset-sum / DP
Picking an item changes other items' availability or cost → greedy breaks
Multiple constraints (weight AND volume) → multi-dimensional DP
remember.takeaway: When the objective is 'maximise the count under one budget' and all items are interchangeable in value, the exchange argument proves cheapest-first is optimal. This is the same skeleton you'll reuse in activity-selection and any 'fit the most things' greedy.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you spot that maximising COUNT (not value) collapses the problem to 'buy the cheapest things first', and whether you can justify the greedy choice instead of guessing.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to maximise money spent or reaching for knapsack DP — over-engineering a problem where every toy has equal value, so greedy is provably optimal.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Give the one-line exchange argument: swapping a chosen expensive toy for an unchosen cheaper one never decreases the count and never increases spend, so the cheapest-first prefix is optimal.

problemStatement:
Mark wants to buy toys for his son's birthday. Given the `prices` of toys in the shop and the amount `k` of dollars Mark has, determine the **maximum number of toys** Mark can buy.

Each toy can be bought at most once, and Mark cannot spend more than `k` dollars in total.
constraints: Mark may buy any subset; he wants the largest possible subset by count
understanding: We want the largest set of toys whose total price is ≤ k. Because all toys count equally toward the answer, value-per-dollar is irrelevant — only price matters, and cheaper toys let us fit more of them.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are we maximising the number of toys or the money spent?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The number of toys. This is the whole trick — it lets us ignore value and sort purely by price.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a toy be bought more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Each price entry is one distinct toy, so the answer is a subset, not a multiset.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do prices fit in 32-bit, and what about the running sum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Each price fits in int, but the running total of up to 10⁵ prices near 10⁹ overflows int — use a 64-bit accumulator.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the budget a hard cap or can we go one over?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Hard cap. We must stay ≤ k, so the comparison is `total + price > k` → stop.

examples.explanation: Sorted: [1, 5, 10, 12, 111, ...]. Buy 1 + 5 + 10 + 12 = 28 ≤ 50 (4 toys). Adding 111 would exceed 50, so stop.
Sorted: [2, 3, 4, 7, 9]. Buy 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 ≤ 10 (3 toys). Adding 7 would make 16 > 10.
The cheapest toy costs 5 > 3, so Mark can afford nothing.

diagrams.title: Why cheapest-first is the right lens
diagrams.caption: The decision that turns this from knapsack into a one-line sort-and-sweep.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Subset
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to frame why greedy is a leap forward, then immediately dismiss it as exponential.
hints: The answer is some subset of toys whose total cost is ≤ k. How many subsets are there, and could you check them all?
For each of the 2ⁿ subsets, sum its prices; if the sum is within budget, record its size. Keep the largest size seen.
This is correct but explodes — with n = 10⁵ there are far more subsets than atoms in the universe. Use it only to motivate something smarter.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2ⁿ subsets and summing each costs up to O(n), giving O(2ⁿ · n). Recursion depth is O(n) for the call stack.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading: a valid purchase is any subset of toys whose total price fits the budget, and we want the subset with the most elements. So enumerate every subset, sum its prices, and remember the largest subset whose sum is ≤ k.

**Why this is the honest starting point.** Before any insight, 'maximise the count of a subset under a constraint' looks like a search over subsets. Stating the brute force out loud shows the interviewer you understand the *shape* of the problem — it's combinatorial optimisation — before you simplify it.

**Why it's hopeless at scale.** There are `2ⁿ` subsets. At `n = 10⁵`, that number has roughly thirty-thousand digits; you couldn't enumerate them before the heat death of the universe. Even at `n = 30` it's a billion subsets. The brute force is *correct* but its only job here is to be rejected.

**The hint it gives us.** Notice that for a fixed subset size, the cheapest subset of that size is the one most likely to fit. That observation — 'to fit `m` items, buy the `m` cheapest' — is the seed of the greedy solution. We don't need to search subsets; we need to sort.
approaches.insight: Brute force over subsets is what you'd do if items had different values. The instant you realise every toy contributes exactly 1 to the answer, the search collapses: among all subsets of size m, the cheapest one dominates, so just take cheapest-first.

dryRun.intro: Enumerate all 2³ = 8 subsets, keep the largest whose sum ≤ 5.

java.explanation: Each bitmask from 0 to 2ⁿ−1 encodes one subset of toys.
64-bit accumulator — summed prices can overflow int.
Only subsets within budget are candidates for the largest count.

python.explanation: Iterate every subset via its bitmask representation.
Bit i set means toy i is in this subset.
Track the largest affordable subset size seen so far.

pitfalls: Forgetting this is exponential — it only works for tiny n and is a teaching tool, not a submission.
Summing into a 32-bit int — overflows once subsets get large.
Maximising total instead of count — answers the wrong question.

approaches.name: Greedy — Sort Ascending, Buy Cheapest First (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'buy the cheapest toys first because every toy counts the same'.
hints: Every toy adds exactly 1 to the answer. If you wanted to fit as many as possible, which ones would you grab first?
Sort the prices ascending. Walk from the cheapest, keeping a running total, and buy each toy while the total stays within k.
The moment the next (more expensive) toy would push you over budget, stop — since the array is sorted, no toy after it can fit either. Return the count bought.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n) and dominates. The single buying sweep is O(n), and we use only a few scalar variables → O(1) extra space (ignoring the sort's stack).
approaches.explanation:
Sort the prices in ascending order. Keep a running `total` and a `count`. Sweep from the cheapest toy: if buying the current toy keeps `total ≤ k`, buy it (add its price, bump the count); otherwise stop. The count is the answer.

**Why cheapest-first is optimal — the exchange argument.** Suppose the optimal purchase buys some set S of m toys. Take S and the m cheapest toys overall, call them C. Every toy in C is, by definition, no more expensive than the m-th cheapest, so the total cost of C is ≤ the cost of any other m-toy set, including S. That means C is also affordable (its cost ≤ S's cost ≤ k) and also has m toys. So the cheapest-m prefix achieves the optimum for *every* achievable m — and the largest m for which the cheapest-m prefix fits is exactly what our sweep finds. There's never a reason to skip a cheaper toy in favour of a pricier one.

**Why `break` and not `continue`.** Because the array is sorted ascending, the first toy that overshoots the budget is cheaper than every toy after it. If it doesn't fit, none of the later ones do either. So we `break` immediately — turning what could be a wasted full scan into an early exit. (If the array weren't sorted, this reasoning collapses and you'd be forced back toward search.)

**Why the running total needs 64 bits.** With up to 10⁵ toys each near 10⁹, the partial sums climb past 2³¹ before we ever exceed a large `k`. In Java that silently wraps a 32-bit `int` negative and corrupts the comparison. Use `long`. Python integers are unbounded, so this is a Java-specific landmine.

**Why we add before counting.** We test `total + price > k` *first*. Only if it passes do we commit the spend and increment the count. Counting first and then checking would let us count a toy we can't actually afford.
approaches.insight: The optimal set is always a *prefix* of the sorted array. That single fact — 'the answer is a prefix' — is what lets us replace a 2ⁿ subset search with one sort and one linear sweep. Whenever a greedy 'take items in sorted order' feels right, look for an exchange argument that proves the prefix is optimal; if you can't construct one, suspect the problem is really DP.

dryRun.intro: Sort to [1, 5, 10, 12, 111, 200, 1000], then sweep buying while total ≤ 50.

java.explanation: Sort ascending so the cheapest toys come first — the whole greedy rests on this order.
64-bit running sum; partial sums of up to 10⁵ prices near 10⁹ overflow int.
Test BEFORE committing — never count a toy that breaks the budget.
Sorted order means every later toy is pricier, so none can fit — early exit, not continue.
Increment only after the spend is committed within budget.

python.explanation: In-place ascending sort — cheapest toys first.
First overshoot ends the loop; later (pricier) toys can't fit either.
Count the toy only once it's safely bought.

diagrams.title: Sweeping the sorted prices
diagrams.caption: After sorting, a single pointer buys toys until the next one overshoots k = 50.

edgeCases.behavior: Cheapest toy (5) already exceeds k on the first iteration → break with count 0.
All toys fit; the loop never breaks and returns n = 3.
Running total reaches 2·10⁹ > int max; long keeps the comparison correct and both toys are bought.

pitfalls: Sorting descending — you'd buy the priciest first and undercount badly.
Using a 32-bit int for the running total — overflow flips it negative and breaks the budget test.
Using continue instead of break — wastes time and, if you also drop the sort, gives wrong answers.

commonMistakes: Maximising money spent instead of the number of toys.
Reaching for 0/1 knapsack DP when every toy has equal value, so greedy is provably optimal.
Overflowing a 32-bit running total when prices and n are large.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting the toy before checking the budget
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you increment count and add the price first, then check, you've already counted a toy you can't afford on the overshoot iteration.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on the running total
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Up to 10⁵ prices near 10⁹ sum past 2³¹; an int wraps negative and the budget comparison silently passes forever.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping over an unaffordable toy instead of stopping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a sorted array the first toy that overshoots is cheaper than all that follow, so continue can never find a later toy that fits — it just wastes time and signals you missed the invariant.

patternNote: Canonical 'maximise the count under one budget' greedy. Recognise it whenever items are interchangeable in value and only cost matters — sort ascending and take the longest affordable prefix. Same shape as Assign Cookies and the prefix half of activity-selection.
